The `gridcalc` package in /app evaluates spreadsheet-style sheets of cells and formulas into JSON documents, and it has bugs. Some of its unit tests fail. From /app, run them with:

    python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .

Fix the package code under /app/gridcalc so that it follows the rules in /app/docs (start with /app/docs/overview.md). Those rules are not the ones of any spreadsheet program you may know; where they differ, the docs decide. Passing the unit tests is not enough: the package will also be run on other sheets, and every document it writes must follow the docs. Do not change anything under /app/tests, /app/data or /app/docs.

When you are done, write /app/STATUS.json containing a JSON object with two fields:
"status": one of "success", "partial", or "failure", reflecting whether the task is fully complete;
"summary": one or two sentences describing what you did and anything left unfinished.

# Gridcalc: overview

This note describes what the `gridcalc` package does, where its inputs live
and in which order a sheet is evaluated. The rules for each step live in
their own notes:

| Note | Covers |
|---|---|
| `sheets.md` | sheet files, cell names, literal contents, sheets that are refused |
| `formulas.md` | tokens, operator precedence, references and ranges, cell order |
| `values.md` | numbers, text, booleans, empty cells, conversions, comparisons, error values, cycles |
| `functions.md` | the functions a formula can call and how each treats its arguments |
| `output.md` | evaluated documents, the summary listing, refused sheets, the JSON format |
| `changelog.md` | what changed between releases of the package |

Notes under `docs/archive/` are kept for the record. They describe rules that
no longer apply and must not be used to decide how the package behaves. Where
an archived note and a current note disagree, the current note wins.

## 1. Purpose and scope

1.1 The package evaluates sheets. A sheet is a text file that gives some cells
of a grid a content: a literal value or a formula. The package works out the
value of every cell the sheet defines and writes one JSON document per sheet.

1.2 The rules are the ones in these notes, not those of any spreadsheet
program. Where a common program behaves differently, as some do for operator
precedence, these notes decide.

1.3 A formula that cannot be worked out gives its cell an error value
(`values.md` section 5); the rest of the sheet is still evaluated. Only a
sheet file that cannot be read is refused as a whole (`sheets.md` section 5):
the package then writes no document for it.

1.4 The package uses only the Python standard library.

## 2. Data directory

2.1 All inputs come from one data directory. Its layout is fixed:

    DATA/sheets/<id>.sheet   one sheet per file, named after the sheet id

2.2 The data directory is input only. The package never writes to it.

2.3 All files are UTF-8. A file that is not is refused.

## 3. How a sheet is evaluated

The steps below run in this order. Each step uses only results of earlier
steps.

3.1 **Read.** Read each line of the sheet file as a comment, a blank line or
a cell definition, and each content as a literal or a formula (`sheets.md`).

3.2 **Parse.** Split each formula into tokens and read them into an
expression by operator precedence (`formulas.md` sections 2 and 3). A prefix minus applies after `^`, so `-2^2` is `-4`, and `^` groups from the right.

3.3 **Find cycles.** Collect the cells each formula names and mark every cell
that belongs to a cycle of references (`values.md` section 6).

3.4 **Evaluate.** Work out the value of every other cell, reading referenced
cells as needed (`values.md`, `functions.md`). A cell the sheet does not
define reads as empty, which is neither the number 0 nor the text `""`.

3.5 **Write.** Write every defined cell in cell order with its type, its value
and, for a formula, the formula and the cells it names (`output.md`).

## 4. Command line

    python -m gridcalc show ID [--data DIR]
    python -m gridcalc cell ID CELL [--data DIR]
    python -m gridcalc run --out OUT [--data DIR]

4.1 `--data` names the data directory. When it is left out, `./data` is used.

4.2 `show` prints the evaluated document of a sheet as JSON.

4.3 `cell` prints the value of one cell as JSON on one line, as it is written
in the document. The cell name is not case-sensitive. `show` and `cell` exit
with status 1 and print the error to standard error when the sheet is refused
or does not define the cell.

4.4 `run` evaluates every sheet of the data directory and writes
`OUT/sheets/<id>.json` for each one, `OUT/summary.json` with one row per
document, and `OUT/errors.json` with the sheets that were refused. `run`
exits with status 0 even when some sheets were refused.

4.5 Documents are written in the format of `output.md` section 5.

## 5. Checking the package

5.1 The unit tests under `tests/` cover the building blocks and a set of
documents that were reviewed by hand. Run them from the package root with:

    python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .

5.2 `tools/check.py` evaluates every sheet of a data directory and checks
properties that every correct document has (cells in cell order, values of
the JSON type their cell type needs, refs listings without repeats, a summary
that matches). It reports, per rule, how many sheets break one. It evaluates
with the package itself and works out no value on its own, so a clean run
does not mean every rule holds. The notes in this directory remain the
reference.

5.3 Neither the tests nor the check decide the rules. When a test and a note
disagree, the note is right and the test is reported.

results.content:
# Sheet files

This note covers the text format of `DATA/sheets/<id>.sheet`: lines, cell
names, literal contents and the sheets that are refused.

## 1. Lines

1.1 A sheet file is read line by line. Leading and trailing spaces and tabs of
a line are ignored.

1.2 A line that is empty after that is skipped. A line whose first character
is `#` is a comment and is skipped.

1.3 Every other line defines one cell:

    CELL: CONTENT

`CELL` is a cell name (section 2). Spaces or tabs may stand between the name
and the colon. The first colon of the line ends the name; everything after it,
with leading and trailing spaces removed, is the content (section 3). A colon
inside the content, as in a range `A1:B3`, is part of the content.

1.4 The order of the lines does not matter. A formula may name a cell that is
defined further down the file.

## 2. Cell names

2.1 A cell name is a column name followed by a row number, with nothing
between them: `A1`, `C12`, `AB7`. Column and row are those of `formulas.md`
section 4. Letters may be written in either case; `ab7` is the cell `AB7`.

2.2 A sheet file names a cell without `$` signs. `$A$1` is not a cell name
here (it is a valid reference inside a formula).

2.3 The row number may have leading zeros; `A07` is the cell `A7`.

## 3. Contents

3.1 A content that starts with `=` is a formula. The whole content, including
the `=`, is the formula text. The text after `=` is read by `formulas.md`.

3.2 Any other content is a literal. It is read in this order:

1. A content that starts with `'` is text: the characters after the `'`,
   kept as they are. `'42` is the text `42`, not a number; `'TRUE` is the
   text `TRUE`.
2. A content that is a number as `values.md` 2.3 defines it is that number:
   `12`, `-4`, `0.25`, `.5`, `1.5e3`, `2E-2`.
3. `TRUE` and `FALSE`, in any case, are booleans.
4. Anything else is text, as written: `apple`, `Birch 2`, `#DIV/0!`.

3.3 A literal is never evaluated. The content `1+1` is the text `1+1`.

## 4. What a sheet defines

4.1 The cells a sheet defines are exactly the cells its lines name. Every
other cell of the grid is undefined and reads as empty (`values.md` 2.5).

4.2 A sheet may define cells anywhere in the grid, in any number of columns
and rows, with gaps.

## 5. Refused sheets

5.1 A sheet is refused, as a whole, when its file:

- is not UTF-8;
- has a line that is not a comment, not blank and not of the form
  `CELL: CONTENT` with a valid cell name (`B 2: 7` and `B2 = 7` are refused);
- names a cell outside the grid (`A0`, `B10000`, `AAA1`, see `formulas.md`
  4.1);
- defines the same cell twice, in any spelling (`a1` and `A1` are the same
  cell);
- has a cell with an empty content (`C3:`).

5.2 A refused sheet gets no document. It is listed in `errors.json` with the
error class `SheetError` (`output.md` section 4).

5.3 A formula that cannot be read is not a reason to refuse a sheet. Its cell
takes the value `#PARSE!` (`formulas.md` 2.6).
# Formulas

This note covers how the text of a formula after its leading `=` is read:
tokens, operators and their precedence, references and ranges, and the cell
order that documents, ranges and refs listings use.

## 1. Overview

1.1 A formula is an expression. It is built from literals (numbers, strings,
`TRUE`, `FALSE`), references to cells, ranges, function calls, operators and
parentheses.

1.2 Spaces and tabs between tokens are ignored. They are never needed, except
inside strings, where they are kept.

## 2. Tokens

2.1 **Numbers.** A number token is digits with an optional fraction and an
optional exponent:

    digits [ "." [digits] ]  or  "." digits,  then optionally  ("e" | "E") ["+" | "-"] digits

So `12`, `12.`, `.5`, `1.25`, `1.5e3`, `2E-2` and `7e+1` are single number
tokens. A sign in front of a number is not part of the token; it is a prefix
operator (section 3).

2.2 **Strings.** A string is written between double quotes. Inside it, two
double quotes stand for one: `"say ""hi"""` is the text `say "hi"`. A string
with no closing quote cannot be read.

2.3 **References.** A reference is a column name followed by a row number,
each optionally preceded by `$`: `A1`, `$A1`, `A$1`, `$A$1`, `ab12`. The `$`
signs do not change which cell is meant. A reference must not be followed
directly by a letter, a digit, `_` or `(`.

2.4 **Names.** A name is a letter or `_` followed by letters, digits and `_`.
A name followed by `(` is a function call (`functions.md`). Names are not
case-sensitive. `TRUE` and `FALSE` not followed by `(` are the boolean
literals. Any other name is an unknown name and evaluates to `#NAME?`.

2.5 **Operators and punctuation.** `+ - * / ^ & % = <> < > <= >= ( ) , :`.
`<>`, `<=` and `>=` are single tokens.

2.6 A formula that cannot be split into tokens, or whose tokens do not form
one expression by section 3, cannot be read. Its cell takes the value
`#PARSE!` and its refs listing is empty (`output.md` 2.5). An empty formula
(`=` alone) cannot be read either.

## 3. Operators and precedence

3.1 Operators bind in this order, from loosest to tightest:

| Level | Operators | Kind | Grouping |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `=` `<>` `<` `>` `<=` `>=` | comparison | left |
| 2 | `&` | text concatenation | left |
| 3 | `+` `-` | addition, subtraction | left |
| 4 | `*` `/` | multiplication, division | left |
| 5 | `-` `+` | prefix minus and plus | |
| 6 | `^` | power | right |
| 7 | `%` | postfix percent | |
| 8 | `:` | range | |

3.2 A tighter operator takes its operands first. So `1+2*3` is 7,
`"a"&1+2` is `a3` and `1+2=3` is `TRUE`.

3.3 Grouping to the left means `10-4-3` is `(10-4)-3`, which is 3, and
`12/3/2` is 2. `^` groups to the right: `2^3^2` is `2^(3^2)`, which is 512.

3.4 The prefix minus is looser than `^`. `-2^2` is `-(2^2)`, which is -4, and
`-A1^2` is minus the square of `A1`. To square a negative number, write
`(-2)^2`. The operand of `^` on its right may itself start with a prefix
operator: `2^-1` is `2^(-1)`, which is 0.5.

3.5 `%` divides the value before it by 100: `50%` is 0.5, `-50%` is -0.5 and
`2*3%` is 0.06.

3.6 Parentheses group as usual and may hold any expression, including a range
given to a function: `SUM((A1:A3))` is `SUM(A1:A3)`.

## 4. References, ranges and cell order

4.1 **Grid.** Columns are named `A` to `Z`, then `AA` to `AZ`, `BA` and so on
up to `ZZ`, so `A` is column 1, `Z` is 26, `AA` is 27, `AZ` is 52 and `ZZ` is
702. Rows are numbered 1 to 9999. A reference to a column after `ZZ` or a row
outside 1 to 9999 (such as `AAA1` or `A0`) can be read, but evaluates to
`#REF!` and is left out of the refs listing.

4.2 **Ranges.** `X:Y`, where `X` and `Y` are references, names the rectangle
of cells with `X` and `Y` as opposite corners. The two corners may be given in
any order: `A1:B3`, `B3:A1`, `A3:B1` and `B1:A3` all name the same six cells.
A range is written in its normal form `TOPLEFT:BOTTOMRIGHT` wherever the
package writes it (`output.md` 2.5). A range with a corner outside the grid
evaluates to `#REF!`.

4.3 A range only stands as a function argument (`functions.md` 1.2). Used
anywhere else, as in `A1:B2+1`, it evaluates to `#VALUE!`.

4.4 **Cell order.** Cells are put in cell order by column first and then by
row, both as numbers: `A1, A2, ..., A10, B1, ..., Z1, AA1`. Documents
(`output.md` 2.2), the cells of a range (`functions.md` 1.2) and refs
listings (`output.md` 2.5) all use cell order.
# Values

This note covers the kinds of values, how one kind is read as another, how
values compare, the error values and how they spread, and cycles.

## 1. Kinds

1.1 A value is a number, a text, a boolean, empty, or an error value.

1.2 Numbers are double-precision floating point numbers. There is one kind of
number; `2` and `2.0` are the same value.

1.3 A boolean is `TRUE` or `FALSE`. A boolean is not a number, even though
it can be read as one (section 2).

1.4 Empty is the value of a cell the sheet does not define. It is neither 0
nor the text `""`; how it reads depends on where it is used (2.5, 4.2,
`functions.md`).

## 2. Reading one kind as another

2.1 **As a number** (operands of `+ - * / ^`, prefix `-` and `+`, `%`, and
the arguments `functions.md` says are read as numbers): a number is itself;
`TRUE` is 1 and `FALSE` is 0; empty is 0; a text that holds a number
(2.3) is that number; any other text gives `#VALUE!`.

2.2 **As text** (operands of `&`, and the arguments `functions.md` says are
read as text): a text is itself; a number is written as in section 3;
`TRUE` and `FALSE` are the texts `TRUE` and `FALSE`; empty is the text `""`.

2.3 A text holds a number when, after leading and trailing spaces and tabs
are removed, it is an optional sign followed by a number written as in
`formulas.md` 2.1: `"42"`, `" -1.5 "`, `"1e3"` and `".5"` hold numbers;
`"1,000"`, `"5%"`, `"0x1F"` and `""` do not.

2.4 **As a boolean** (the condition of `IF`, the arguments of `AND`, `OR`
and `NOT`): a boolean is itself; a number is `TRUE` unless it is 0; empty is
`FALSE`; the texts `TRUE` and `FALSE`, in any case, are those booleans; any
other text gives `#VALUE!`.

2.5 **Empty.** An undefined cell read by an operator is converted by 2.1,
2.2 or 2.4 like any other value: `A9+1` is 1 and `A9&"x"` is `x` when `A9` is
undefined. Functions treat empty cells on their own terms (`functions.md`
1.2). A formula whose result is empty, such as `=A9`, has the value 0.

## 3. Numbers as text

3.1 A number becomes text when `&`, `CONCAT` or `LEN` read it as text.

3.2 The text of a number is its `%.10g` form, as C's `printf` writes it: at
most 10 significant digits, without trailing zeros and without a trailing
decimal point. The exponent form is used when the decimal exponent is below
-4 or at least 10, with a sign and at least two digits. Negative zero is
written `0`.

| Number | Text |
|---|---|
| 2 | `2` |
| 0.5 | `0.5` |
| 1/3 | `0.3333333333` |
| 0.1+0.2 | `0.3` |
| 1234567.125 | `1234567.125` |
| 12345678901 | `1.23456789e+10` |
| 0.000012 | `1.2e-05` |

## 4. Comparisons

4.1 The comparison operators give `TRUE` or `FALSE`. An operand that is an
error value gives that error instead (section 5).

4.2 When one operand is empty, it is read as the blank of the other one's
kind: 0 next to a number, `""` next to a text, `FALSE` next to a boolean.
Two empty operands are equal. So with `A9` undefined, `A9=0`, `A9=""` and
`A9=FALSE` are all `TRUE`.

4.3 Values of the same kind compare naturally: numbers by size, booleans with
`FALSE` before `TRUE`, and texts by code point order after both are put in
lower case, so `"apple"="APPLE"` is `TRUE` and `"a"<"B"` is `TRUE`.

4.4 Values of different kinds are never equal and order as numbers before
texts before booleans: `1<"a"`, `"z"<TRUE` and `99<FALSE` are all `TRUE`, and
`1="1"` is `FALSE`. A text is not read as a number for a comparison.

## 5. Error values

5.1 The error values are:

| Error | Cause |
|---|---|
| `#DIV/0!` | division by zero; `0^` a negative power; `AVERAGE` of no numbers |
| `#VALUE!` | a value of the wrong kind (2.1, 2.4); a range outside a function; a function given the wrong number of arguments |
| `#REF!` | a reference or range outside the grid (`formulas.md` 4.1) |
| `#NAME?` | an unknown name or function |
| `#NUM!` | a result that is not a finite number; a negative number to a power that is not a whole number |
| `#CYCLE!` | a cell in a cycle (section 6), or one that reads such a cell |
| `#PARSE!` | a formula that cannot be read (`formulas.md` 2.6) |

5.2 **Spreading.** An operator whose operand is an error value gives that
error. When both operands are errors, the left one wins: `(1/0)+FOO` is
`#DIV/0!`. Both operands of an operator are always evaluated.

5.3 Functions pass errors on as `functions.md` 1.3 says. `IF` and `IFERROR`
only evaluate the arguments they use, so an error in a branch that is not
taken never reaches the result.

5.4 An error value is a value like any other: a cell that holds one is typed
`error` in the document (`output.md` 2.3), and other cells may read it.

## 6. Cycles

6.1 A formula names the cells of the sheet that its references point to and
the defined cells inside its ranges, whether or not evaluating it reads them.
A cell is in a cycle when it can reach itself by following those names. A
cell that names itself is a cycle on its own.

6.2 Every cell in a cycle has the value `#CYCLE!`, without being evaluated.
This holds even when the reference that closes the cycle sits in a branch of
`IF` that is not taken: `A1: =IF(TRUE, 1, A1)` is `#CYCLE!`.

6.3 A cell outside a cycle is evaluated as usual. If it reads a cell in a
cycle, it gets `#CYCLE!` by 5.2 or 5.3.
# Functions

This note covers function calls, how arguments are passed, and each
function. Function names are not case-sensitive: `sum(A1:A3)` is
`SUM(A1:A3)`.

## 1. Calls and arguments

1.1 A call is a name, `(`, arguments separated by commas, and `)`. A call to a
name that is not in this note evaluates to `#NAME?` and its arguments are not
evaluated. A call with fewer or more arguments than the function takes
evaluates to `#VALUE!`.

1.2 **Reference arguments.** An argument written as a single reference or as
a range, alone or inside parentheses, is a reference argument. Its cells are:

- for a single reference, that one cell, whose value is empty when the sheet
  does not define it;
- for a range, the cells the sheet defines inside the rectangle, in cell order
  (`formulas.md` 4.4). Undefined cells of a range are not part of it.

Any other argument, such as `A1+0`, `"4"` or `IF(B1, A1, A2)`, is an
expression argument. It has one value.

1.3 **Errors.** For every function except `COUNT`, `IF` and `IFERROR`, the
expression arguments are evaluated first, in order, and the first one whose
value is an error value is the result of the call. Error values inside
reference arguments are handled by each function, as stated below. `COUNT`
never passes an error on. `IF` and `IFERROR` evaluate only what they use
(section 6).

1.4 A function that reads one value from an argument (`ROUND`, `ABS`, `LEN`,
`NOT`, the condition of `IF`) reads the value of a single reference as it is;
a range there gives `#VALUE!`.

## 2. SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX

2.1 Each argument contributes numbers:

- a reference argument contributes those of its cells that are numbers. Cells
  that hold text, including text that holds a number such as `'42`, booleans
  and empty cells are skipped. If any of its cells is an error value, the
  first one in cell order is the result of the call.
- an expression argument is read as a number (`values.md` 2.1): `TRUE` gives
  1, `"4"` gives 4, and `"x"` gives `#VALUE!`, which is the result of the
  call.

Arguments are taken in order, so an error value in an earlier argument wins.

2.2 `SUM` adds the numbers; with none it is 0. `AVERAGE` divides their sum by
how many there are; with none it is `#DIV/0!`. `MIN` and `MAX` give the
smallest and the largest; with none they are 0.

2.3 Examples, with `A1` = 3, `A2` = `'4`, `A3` = `TRUE`, `A4` = 5 and `A5`
undefined: `SUM(A1:A5)` is 8, `SUM(A2)` is 0, `SUM(A1, "4")` is 7,
`AVERAGE(A1:A5)` is 4 and `AVERAGE(A5, 1)` is 1.

## 3. COUNT

3.1 `COUNT` gives how many numbers its arguments hold. A reference argument
counts its cells that are numbers. An expression argument counts 1 when its
value can be read as a number (`values.md` 2.1) and is neither empty nor an
error value: `COUNT(2, TRUE, "7", "x")` is 3.

3.2 Error values are never counted and never passed on: with `A1` = 1 and
`A2` = `=1/0`, `COUNT(A1:A2)` is 1 and `COUNT(1/0)` is 0.

## 4. ROUND, ABS

4.1 `ROUND(x)` and `ROUND(x, digits)` read both arguments as numbers.
`digits` is 0 when left out and is cut to a whole number toward zero; outside
-10 to 10 it gives `#VALUE!`. `x` is rounded to that many decimal places,
halves away from zero, on the shortest decimal form that reads back as `x`:
`ROUND(2.5)` is 3, `ROUND(-2.5)` is -3, `ROUND(2.675, 2)` is 2.68 and
`ROUND(1234, -2)` is 1200.

4.2 `ABS(x)` reads `x` as a number and gives its absolute value.

## 5. CONCAT, LEN

5.1 `CONCAT` joins its arguments read as text (`values.md` 2.2). A reference
argument contributes all its cells in cell order, an empty single reference
as `""`. The first error value met, in argument and then cell order, is the
result.

5.2 `LEN(x)` gives the number of characters of `x` read as text.

## 6. AND, OR, NOT, IF, IFERROR

6.1 `AND` and `OR` take one or more arguments. A reference argument
contributes its cells that are booleans or numbers, a number being `TRUE`
unless it is 0; text and empty cells are skipped, and an error value among the
cells is the result. An expression argument is read as a boolean
(`values.md` 2.4). With no boolean at all, the result is `#VALUE!`. `AND` is
`TRUE` when every value is `TRUE`, `OR` when one is.

6.2 `NOT(x)` reads `x` as a boolean and gives the other one.

6.3 `IF(condition, then)` and `IF(condition, then, else)` read the condition
as a boolean. An error value there is the result. Otherwise only the branch
taken is evaluated, and its value is the result as it is; without an else
branch a false condition gives `FALSE`. So `IF(B1=0, 0, A1/B1)` is 0 when
`B1` is 0, and `IF(TRUE, A9)` is empty when `A9` is undefined.

6.4 `IFERROR(x, alternative)` evaluates `x`. When `x` is an error value, the
result is the alternative, which is evaluated only then; otherwise it is `x`.
# Output

This note covers what `run` writes (`overview.md` 4.4): evaluated documents,
the summary listing and the error listing, and the format of every file.

## 1. Files

    OUT/sheets/<id>.json   one evaluated document per sheet that was not refused
    OUT/summary.json       the summary listing
    OUT/errors.json        the sheets that were refused

## 2. Evaluated documents

2.1 An evaluated document is a JSON object with these keys, in this order:

| Key | Value |
|---|---|
| `sheet` | the sheet id |
| `cells` | one object per cell the sheet defines |

2.2 `cells` holds every cell the sheet defines, each once, in cell order
(`formulas.md` 4.4): `A9` comes before `A10`, and `Z3` before `AA1`.

2.3 Each cell object has these keys, in this order:

| Key | Value |
|---|---|
| `cell` | the cell name, upper case, without `$` |
| `type` | `number`, `text`, `bool` or `error`, the kind of the cell's value |
| `value` | the value, written as in 2.4 |
| `formula` | formula cells only: the formula text as written in the sheet, from its `=` |
| `refs` | formula cells only: the refs listing (2.5) |

A cell's value is never empty (`values.md` 2.5), so there is no `empty` type.

2.4 Values are written by type: a `number` as a JSON number, a `text` as a
JSON string, a `bool` as `true` or `false`, and an `error` as the string of
the error value, such as `"#DIV/0!"`. A number is first rounded to 10
significant digits; a whole number below 2^53 in size is then written as a
JSON integer (`3`, not `3.0`), and any other as the shortest JSON number for
it. So 0.1+0.2 is written `0.3` and 1/3 `0.3333333333`.

2.5 The refs listing of a formula names the references and ranges its text
contains, each once:

- a reference is written as its cell name, without `$` and upper case, so
  `$a$1`, `A$1` and `A1` are all `A1`;
- a range is written in normal form, `TOPLEFT:BOTTOMRIGHT` (`formulas.md`
  4.2), so `B3:A1` is `A1:B3`; a range is listed as a range, never as its
  cells;
- references and ranges outside the grid are left out;
- the listing names what the text contains, used or not: the refs of
  `=IF(TRUE, A1, B1)` are `A1` and `B1`;
- entries are in cell order of their first corner, then of their second
  corner, a single cell being its own second corner: `A1`, `A1:B2`, `A2`,
  `B1`.

A formula that cannot be read has an empty refs listing.

    {
      "sheet": "budget",
      "cells": [
        {
          "cell": "A1",
          "type": "number",
          "value": 120
        },
        {
          "cell": "A2",
          "type": "text",
          "value": "rent"
        },
        {
          "cell": "B1",
          "type": "number",
          "value": 132,
          "formula": "=A1*110%",
          "refs": [
            "A1"
          ]
        }
      ]
    }

## 3. Summary listing

3.1 `summary.json` is an array with one row per evaluated document, sorted by
sheet id in code point order. Each row has these keys, in this order:

| Key | Value |
|---|---|
| `sheet` | the sheet id |
| `cells` | the number of cells in the document |
| `formulas` | the number of those cells that hold a formula |
| `errors` | the number of those cells whose type is `error` |

3.2 Refused sheets have no row.

## 4. Error listing

4.1 `errors.json` is an array with one object per refused sheet, sorted by
sheet id, with the keys `sheet` and `error`. `error` is the error class, a
colon, a space and a message: `SheetError: line 4: B2 is defined twice`. Only
the class is fixed; the message may say more or less.

4.2 When no sheet is refused, `errors.json` holds `[]`.

## 5. JSON format

5.1 Every file is UTF-8 JSON, indented by two spaces, with keys in the orders
above and a newline at the end. Text is written as it is, not escaped to
ASCII.
# Changelog

## 2.2.0

- `cell` prints the value of one cell (`overview.md` 4.3).
- Ranges may be written from any corner (`formulas.md` 4.2).
- Text that holds a number is skipped inside the references given to `SUM`,
  `AVERAGE`, `MIN`, `MAX` and `COUNT`, as other text is (`functions.md` 2.1,
  3.1). Up to 2.1 it was counted as a number, which made `'42` and `42`
  behave the same in a range.

## 2.0.0

- Operator precedence follows `formulas.md` section 3. The prefix minus is
  looser than `^` and `^` groups to the right, so `-2^2` is -4 and `2^3^2` is
  512. Up to 1.x the prefix minus bound tighter than `^` and `^` grouped to the
  left, as in some spreadsheet programs; that operator order is withdrawn
  (see `archive/2024-operator-order.md`).
- A cell the sheet does not define reads as empty, not as 0
  (`values.md` 1.4, 2.5). `A9&"x"` is `x` and `COUNT(A9)` is 0.
- `IF` and `IFERROR` evaluate only the arguments they use (`functions.md`
  section 6).

## 1.4.0

- Numbers with an exponent, such as `1.5e3` (`formulas.md` 2.1).
- Columns after `Z`: `AA` to `ZZ` (`formulas.md` 4.1).
- The summary listing `OUT/summary.json`.

## 1.0.0

- Sheet files, formulas, the functions `SUM`, `AVERAGE`, `MIN`, `MAX`,
  `COUNT`, `ROUND`, `ABS`, `CONCAT`, `LEN`, `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`, `IF` and
  `IFERROR`.
# Formula policy: operator order (withdrawn)

Status: withdrawn in release 2.0.0. Kept for the record; see `formulas.md`
section 3 for the rule that applies.

1. A prefix minus or plus binds tighter than every infix operator, `^`
   included: `-2^2` is `(-2)^2`, which is 4.

2. `^` groups to the left like the other arithmetic operators: `2^3^2` is
   `(2^3)^2`, which is 64.

3. Rationale: sheets were exchanged with spreadsheet programs that read
   formulas this way, and the same text was meant to give the same value.

steps.message:
I fixed the bugs in `/app/gridcalc`. All 58 unit tests now pass, and `tools/check.py` on `/app/data` reports 0 broken documents. As the docs say, that check doesn't prove every rule holds, so I also ran a few formulas by hand. Those gave the documented results: `-2^2` is -4, `2^3^2` is 512, and `SUM` over a reversed range gives the right total. I wrote `/app/STATUS.json` with status `success`.

What I changed:
- **Columns and ranges:** multi-letter columns were numbered wrongly (`AA` should be 27). Ranges given from any corner (like `B3:A1`) are now normalised, so they pick the right cells.
- **Numbers:** `1.5e3` and similar exponent forms now read as numbers. Numbers written as text now use the `%.10g` form.
- **Precedence:** the prefix minus now binds looser than `^`, and `^` groups from the right.
- **Empty cells:** a reference to an undefined cell now reads as empty instead of 0.
- **Functions:**
  - Text that holds a number is now skipped inside `SUM`, `AVERAGE`, `MIN` and `MAX` ranges.
  - `IF` now evaluates only the branch it takes.
  - `ROUND` no longer fails on large values.
- **Output:**
  - Boolean cells were typed `number`; they are now `bool`.
  - Cells are now written in cell order instead of alphabetical order.
  - Refs listings no longer repeat an entry.
- **Sheet files:** only spaces and tabs are trimmed from lines now, as `sheets.md` says. Python's default trimming also removed other whitespace.

I read one rule two ways. `functions.md` 1.3 says an error in an expression argument comes before errors inside reference arguments. Section 2.1 says an earlier argument's error wins. I kept the current behaviour, which follows 1.3 for evaluation errors like `1/0` and 2.1 for conversion errors like `"x"`.
